content: Chronic ear infection refers to the presence of fluid, swelling, or infection behind the eardrum that either persists over time or recurs frequently, potentially leading to long-term or permanent damage to the ear. Symptoms of Chronic Ear Infection: Chronic ear infections often present with less severe symptoms compared to acute infections, which may result in delayed recognition and treatment. Low-grade fever may be present. Young infants may exhibit fussiness or irritability. Pus-like drainage from the ear is a common sign. Hearing loss may occur, which can be temporary or persistent. Symptoms may either persist continuously or fluctuate, and they can affect one or both ears. Causes of Chronic Ear Infection: The eustachian tube, which connects the middle ear to the back of the throat, is responsible for draining fluid from the middle ear. If this tube becomes blocked, fluid accumulation can occur, creating an environment conducive to infection. Chronic ear infections may result from an acute ear infection that fails to resolve completely or from repeated episodes of ear infections. The term suppurative chronic otitis is used to describe a condition where the eardrum repeatedly ruptures, drains, or swells in the middle ear or mastoid region without resolution. Risk Factors: Children are more prone to ear infections due to the anatomical characteristics of their eustachian tubes, which are shorter, narrower, and more horizontal compared to adults. Chronic ear infections are less common than acute ear infections. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider will perform an ear examination, which may reveal: Dullness or redness in the middle ear. Air bubbles or thick fluid in the middle ear. The eardrum may appear adhered to the bones of the middle ear. Fluid drainage from the eardrum. A perforation (hole) in the eardrum. The eardrum may bulge outward or collapse inward. Additional diagnostic tests may include: Cultures of the fluid to identify bacteria, which may be resistant or more difficult to treat than those causing acute infections. CT scans of the head or mastoid region to assess the spread of infection beyond the middle ear. Hearing tests to evaluate the extent of hearing loss. When to Seek Medical Attention: Contact a healthcare provider if you or your child exhibit signs of a chronic ear infection. Seek medical care if an ear infection does not respond to treatment or if new symptoms develop during or after treatment. Treatment Options: Antibiotics may be prescribed if the infection is bacterial in origin. Long-term antibiotic therapy, either orally or intravenously, may be necessary. If there is a perforation in the eardrum, antibiotic ear drops may be used. For infections that are difficult to treat and involve a perforated eardrum, a dilute acidic solution (e.g., distilled vinegar and water) may be recommended. Surgical interventions may be required, including: Mastoidectomy: Surgery to remove infection from the mastoid bone. Ossicular chain reconstruction: Surgery to repair or replace the small bones in the middle ear. Tympanoplasty: Repair of the eardrum. Ear tube surgery to facilitate drainage and prevent fluid buildup. Prognosis: Chronic ear infections generally respond well to treatment, although prolonged medication use may be necessary. While not life-threatening, chronic ear infections can cause discomfort and may lead to hearing loss or other complications. Potential Complications: Chronic ear infections can result in permanent structural changes to the ear and surrounding bones, including: Mastoiditis: Infection of the mastoid bone behind the ear. Persistent drainage from a perforated eardrum, even after ear tube placement. Cholesteatoma: A cyst in the middle ear. Tympanosclerosis: Hardening of tissue in the middle ear. Erosion or damage to the middle ear bones, impairing hearing. Facial paralysis. Epidural abscess or brain inflammation. Damage to the balance-regulating structures of the ear. Hearing loss, whether partial or complete, can lead to delayed speech or language development, particularly in cases where both ears are affected. Permanent hearing loss is rare but becomes more likely with prolonged or recurrent infections. Prevention: Prompt treatment of acute ear infections can reduce the risk of progression to chronic ear infections.
